newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Thirst for energy seen stoking Asian coal imports.
newsitem.headline: Thirst for energy seen stoking Asian coal imports.

text.p: Fast-growing Asia is expected to increase coal imports sharply by the turn of the century to feed its thirst for power, an industry official said on Tuesday.
Graeme Robertson, vice-chairman of the Indonesian Coal Association and director of the World Coal Institute, said European imports, however, were expected to grow only marginally.

Imports by Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong were projected to hit 124.5 million tonnes in 1996 from 113.1 million tonnes in 1995, and soar to 152 million tonnes in 1999 and 179.5 million tonnes in 2002.
Robertson said imports by the Philippines, Thailand and Malaysia were expected to more than double to 13.9 million tonnes in 1999 from an estimated 6.7 million tonnes in 1996.
"Imports by China and India are expected to rise to 21 million tonnes in 1999 from an estimated eight million tonnes in 1996," he told Reuters in an interview.
He said imports by European countries were expected to grow to 81 million tonnes in 1999 from about 72 million in 1996.
"South Korea, Japan and Taiwan will be adding 7,000 megawatts of electricity produced by coal-fired plants which will come on stream by mid to second-half 1997," he said.

He said similar projects were also coming on stream or being planned in the Philippines, Thailand, China, India and Indonesia, the world's third largest coal exporter after Australia and South Africa.

Robertson, who is also chairman and chief executive officer of the Swabara Group which has interests ranging from coal mining to power generation and financial services, said the first phase of Indonesia's Paiton power project will become operational in 1998 and the second in 1999.

All of the electricity produced by the first phase of the 1,230-MW Paiton plant, touted as one of the archipelago's biggest private infrastructure projects, would be bought by state utility giant, PT Perusahaan Listrik Negara.
Robertson said two more coal-fired power plants were under construction, five others were in the negotiation stage, while another five projects were set to begin construction in Indonesia.
He said Indonesia was an important source of coal for the Asian market, but added that domestic consumption would place a ceiling on the level of its exports.
Robertson said coal production by Indonesian companies was expected to rise to more than 90 million tonnes by 2002 from nearly 42 million tonnes in 1995.
He also said approval of several applications for contracts of work by coal companies had been delayed by the government pending settlement of the huge Busang gold find in Kalimantan.

"Several applications made in June or July last year and last December have been delayed pending settlement of the Busang area," he said. "I hope coal contracts can be separated from gold contracts of work, and hope it can be settled quickly."

The Indonesian government has given Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd and Barrick Gold Corp one month from January 17 to settle with their local partners before getting the green light to jointly develop the find, estimated by Bre-X to contain at least 57 million ounces of gold worth over $21 billion at current prices.
The find has been mired in controversy following government intervention and conflicting ownership claims.
